claim: The weakest backgrounds that decrease the gain of retinal output signals are similar to those that increase human behavioral threshold.
source: We find that the weakest backgrounds that decrease the gain of the retinal output signals are similar to those that increase human behavioral threshold
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract and supported by experimental data comparing retinal ganglion cell responses to human behavioral thresholds throughout the manuscript.

claim: The gain of retinal signals begins to decrease essentially as soon as background lights are detectable.
source: the gain of retinal signals begins to decrease essentially as soon as background lights are detectable
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experimental measurements showing gain changes at ~0.02 R*/rod/s, which corresponds to detectable backgrounds.

claim: Under conditions where backgrounds are just detectable, gain control does not rely on a highly averaged estimate of the photon count.
source: under these conditions, gain control does not rely on a highly averaged estimate of the photon count, but instead signals from individual photon absorptions trigger changes in gain
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing rapid gain changes and modeling indicating single photon absorptions affect gain.

claim: Signals from individual photon absorptions trigger changes in gain at low backgrounds.
source: signals from individual photon absorptions trigger changes in gain
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments showing gain changes occur with minimal photon counts and modeling of single photon effects.

claim: A rock concert is approximately 10^12 times louder than a just detectable whisper.
source: a rock concert is ∼1012 times louder than a just detectable whisper
evidence: This is stated as an example of the dynamic range sensory systems must encode.

claim: Visual neurons can experience >1000-fold changes in input a few times a second as the eyes move to explore a typical scene.
source: visual neurons can experience >1000-fold changes in input a few times a second as the eyes move to explore a typical scene (Frazor and Geisler, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Frazor and Geisler, 2006.

claim: Standard cameras fail to capture the full structure of scenes with large dynamic range because they employ a single global gain control in the form of an exposure setting.
source: Standard cameras fail to capture the full structure of such scenes because they employ a single global gain control in the form of an exposure setting, which is often poorly matched to the brightest and dimmest regions of a scene
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to illustrate the sophistication of biological sensory gain controls.

claim: Human behavioral threshold begins to increase for backgrounds producing approximately 0.01 isomerized rhodopsin molecules per rod per second.
source: Human behavioral threshold begins to increase for backgrounds producing ∼0.01 isomerized rhodopsin molecules per rod per second (R*/rod/s) (reviewed by Donner, 1992)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review by Donner, 1992.

claim: Several studies suggest that weak backgrounds decrease the gain of retinal signals.
source: several studies suggest that weak backgrounds decrease the gain of retinal signals (Donner, 1992; Brown and Rudd, 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Donner, 1992 and Brown and Rudd, 1998.

claim: Rod-mediated signals traverse the retina through the specialized rod bipolar pathway: rods → rod bipolar cells → AII amacrine cells → cone bipolar cells → ganglion cells.
source: rod-mediated signals traverse the retina through the specialized rod bipolar pathway: rods → rod bipolar cells → AII amacrine cells → cone bipolar cells → ganglion cells
evidence: This pathway is described in text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Mechanisms controlling the gain of rod-mediated signals have been identified within the phototransduction cascade in the rods themselves.
source: Mechanisms controlling the gain of rod-mediated signals have been identified within the phototransduction cascade in the rods themselves (Schneeweis and Schnapf, 2000; Dunn and Rieke, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schneeweis and Schnapf, 2000 and Dunn and Rieke, 2006.

claim: Mechanisms controlling the gain of rod-mediated signals have been identified at the synapse between rod bipolar cells and AII amacrine cells.
source: at the synapse between rod bipolar cells and AII amacrine cells (Dunn and Rieke, 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dunn and Rieke, 2008.

claim: On parasol ganglion cells provide information to cortical circuits about subtle changes in contrast.
source: On parasol ganglion cells provide information to cortical circuits about subtle changes in contrast (Kaplan and Shapley, 1982)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kaplan and Shapley, 1982.

claim: On parasol ganglion cells receive abundant rod-mediated input at low light levels.
source: receive abundant rod-mediated input at low light levels (Purpura et al., 1988; Field et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Purpura et al., 1988 and Field et al., 2009.

claim: On parasol cells are likely to contribute critically to vision at low light levels.
source: these cells are likely to contribute critically to vision at low light levels
evidence: This is inferred from their properties of receiving abundant rod input and providing contrast information.

claim: The effect of changes in background on a cell's spike output is dominated by the changes in excitatory input.
source: Figure 2C,D suggest that the effect of changes in background on a cell's spike output is dominated by the changes in excitatory input
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 2C,D showing parallel changes in excitatory input and spike output.

claim: Detection thresholds for spike responses and excitatory synaptic inputs measured in the same cell were near identical across a range of backgrounds.
source: Detection thresholds for spike responses and excitatory synaptic inputs measured in the same cell were near identical across a range of backgrounds (Figure 2E)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E with data points falling near the unity line.

claim: Inhibitory synaptic inputs to the same stimuli were three to four times smaller than the excitatory inputs.
source: inhibitory synaptic inputs to the same stimuli were three to four times smaller than the excitatory inputs
evidence: This is stated based on measurements, though the data is not shown.

claim: Inhibitory inputs are unlikely to contribute strongly to spike output.
source: hence unlikely to contribute strongly to spike output
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that inhibitory inputs are much smaller than excitatory inputs.

claim: Changes in human behavioral threshold with background show a 'dark light' region extending to approximately 0.01 R*/rod/s in which threshold is independent of background.
source: a 'dark light' region extending to ∼0.01 R*/rod/s in which threshold is independent of background
evidence: This is described as a characteristic region of human behavioral threshold curves, supported by citations.

claim: Changes in human behavioral threshold with background show a 'Rose–deVries' region in which threshold increases with the square root of the background.
source: a 'Rose–deVries' region in which threshold increases with the square root of the background (de Vries, 1943; Rose, 1948)
evidence: This is described as a characteristic region with citations to de Vries, 1943 and Rose, 1948.

claim: Changes in human behavioral threshold with background show a 'Weber' region in which threshold increases proportionally with the background.
source: a 'Weber' region in which threshold increases proportionally with the background
evidence: This is described as a characteristic region of human behavioral threshold curves.

claim: Gain began to decrease for backgrounds near 0.01 or 0.02 R*/rod/s.
source: gain began to decrease for backgrounds near 0.01 or 0.02 R*/rod/s
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and stated in the text based on experimental measurements.

claim: The onset of gain changes occurs close to the onset of changes in human behavioral threshold.
source: close to the onset of changes in human behavioral threshold
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the background levels at which gain changes occur (~0.02 R*/rod/s) with those affecting behavioral threshold (~0.01 R*/rod/s).

claim: Over a ~1000-fold range of backgrounds, gain closely followed Weber law behavior.
source: over a ∼1000-fold range of backgrounds gain closely followed Weber law behavior
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3A showing gain scaling inversely with background over a wide range.

claim: Multiple mechanisms contribute to gain control across the range of backgrounds tested.
source: even though multiple mechanisms contribute to gain control across this range
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of different gain control sites and their engagement at different background levels.

claim: Gain scaled inversely with background above 0.3 R*/rod/s.
source: Gain scaled inversely with background above 0.3 R*/rod/s
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D with slope near -1 for the highest background region.

claim: Noise changed less than 10-fold over a range of backgrounds that produced an approximately 10,000-fold change in gain.
source: noise changed <10-fold over a range of backgrounds that produced an ∼10,000-fold change in gain
evidence: This is stated based on measurements shown in Figure 3B,E.

claim: If Poisson fluctuations dominated noise and gain remained constant, the standard deviation of the current should increase as the square root of the background.
source: If Poisson fluctuations dominated noise and gain remained constant, the standard deviation of the current should increase as the square root of the background—that is, with slope 0.5—since the variance of a Poisson process is proportional to the mean
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the statistical properties of Poisson processes.

claim: Noise changed much less with background than predicted by Poisson fluctuations alone.
source: Noise changed much less with background than this prediction (Figure 3B,E)
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing measured noise changes to theoretical predictions in Figure 3B,E.

claim: The largest increases in noise occurred between darkness and backgrounds <0.01 R*/rod/s.
source: The largest increases in noise occurred between darkness and backgrounds <0.01 R*/rod/s
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The reduction in noise at backgrounds higher than 0.1 R*/rod/s likely reflects the stronger decrease in gain at these backgrounds.
source: The reduction in noise at backgrounds higher than 0.1 R*/rod/s likely reflects the stronger decrease in gain at these backgrounds, which more than compensates the increase in Poisson fluctuations
evidence: This is inferred from the relationship between gain changes and noise measurements.

claim: The threshold for On parasol responses increased for backgrounds as low as 0.02 R*/rod/s.
source: The threshold for On parasol responses increased for backgrounds as low as 0.02 R*/rod/s
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C,F based on experimental measurements.

claim: The threshold increase at 0.02 R*/rod/s corresponds closely with backgrounds that produce changes in behavioral threshold.
source: in close correspondence with backgrounds that produce changes in behavioral threshold (Donner, 1992)
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the measured threshold changes to cited behavioral data.

claim: Threshold increased with a slope <1 for backgrounds between 0.02 and 5 R*/rod/s.
source: Threshold increased with a slope <1 for backgrounds between 0.02 and 5 R*/rod/s (Figure 3F)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F based on experimental measurements.

claim: Gain at low backgrounds is controlled by the mean photon absorption rate and not by the magnitude of the fluctuations about the mean rate.
source: gain at low backgrounds is controlled by the mean photon absorption rate and not by the magnitude of the fluctuations about the mean rate
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fluctuating background experiment in Figure 4.

claim: A gain control that directly depends on the magnitude of the noise would cause gain to scale inversely with the square root of the background.
source: a gain control that directly depends on the magnitude of the noise would cause gain to scale inversely with the square root of the background (Brown and Rudd, 1998)
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction cited from Brown and Rudd, 1998.

claim: The baseline firing rate and mean excitatory input changed slowly following a change in background and had not reached an obvious steady-state level even after 200 s.
source: The baseline firing rate and mean excitatory input changed slowly following a change in background, and had not reached an obvious steady-state level even after 200 s
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gain changes occurred within a few seconds following a change in background.
source: Gain changes, however, occurred within a few seconds following a change in background
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gain changes following an increase in background had a time constant of approximately 0.3 s.
source: time constant of approximately 0.3 s
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B,C based on exponential fits to the data.

claim: Gain changes following a decrease in background had a time constant of approximately 0.5 s.
source: time constant of approximately 0.5 s
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B,C based on exponential fits to the data.

claim: In the 0.1 s following an increase in background from 0.02 to 0.08 R*/rod/s, less than 1 in 100 rods absorbs a photon.
source: in the 0.1 s following an increase in background from 0.02 to 0.08 R*/rod/s, <1 in 100 rods absorbs a photon
evidence: This is calculated from the background intensity and integration time.

claim: The observed gain changes cannot be explained by a mechanism operating on a small collection of rods.
source: the observed gain changes cannot be explained by a mechanism operating on a small collection of rods
evidence: This is inferred from the calculation that very few rods absorb photons in the relevant time window.

claim: The halving of gain produced by a step in background from 0.02 to 0.08 R*/rod/s requires a mechanism that integrates over at least 50 rods.
source: The halving of gain produced by this step in background requires a mechanism that integrates over at least 50 rods even if a single absorbed photon reduces gain to 0
evidence: This is calculated based on the photon absorption statistics and the observed gain change.

claim: Gain changes transferred completely or near completely for bar widths up to 50 µm.
source: Gain changes transferred completely or near completely for bar widths up to 50 µm
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B based on experimental measurements.

claim: Near-complete adaptation transfer at 50 µm bar width requires that the receptive field of the adapting mechanism have a diameter of at least 100 µm.
source: Near-complete adaptation transfer at this bar width requires that the receptive field of the adapting mechanism have a diameter of at least 100 µm
evidence: This is inferred from the logic of the experimental design illustrated in Figure 7B.

claim: A receptive field of 100 µm diameter would contain at least 500 rods given the rod density of approximately 0.1/µm².
source: A receptive field of this size would contain at least 500 rods given the rod density of ∼0.1/µm2 (Osterberg, 1935)
evidence: This is calculated from the receptive field size and cited rod density.

claim: Bar widths of 100 µm and larger produced incomplete adaptation transfer.
source: Bar widths of 100 µm and larger produced incomplete adaptation transfer
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B based on experimental measurements.

claim: Gain control is mediated by a mechanism that has access to signals from hundreds of rods.
source: gain control is mediated by a mechanism that has access to signals from hundreds of rods
evidence: This is concluded from the spatial adaptation transfer experiments in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The degree of spatial pooling required for rapid gain control kinetics is present only downstream of the synapse between rod bipolar cells and AII amacrine cells.
source: This degree of spatial pooling is required to support the rapid kinetics described in Figure 5 and is present only downstream of the synapse between rod bipolar cells and AII amacrine cells (Figure 1)
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the required convergence to the known anatomy of the rod bipolar pathway shown in Figure 1.

claim: Backgrounds that produced substantial reductions in gain of the rod-mediated signals failed to reduce the gain of the cone-mediated signals.
source: Backgrounds that produced substantial reductions in gain of the rod-mediated signals failed to reduce the gain of the cone-mediated signals (Figure 9B–E)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9B-E based on experimental measurements separating rod and cone responses.

claim: Gain changes do not transfer from the rod pathway to the cone pathway.
source: gain changes do not transfer from the rod pathway to the cone pathway
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments in Figure 9 showing differential effects on rod vs cone signals.

claim: Gain is controlled at a site prior to mixing of rod and cone signals in the cone bipolar cell.
source: indicating that gain is controlled at a site prior to mixing of rod and cone signals in the cone bipolar cell
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of transfer of gain changes from rod to cone pathways.

claim: The lack of transfer from rod to cone pathways, together with the requirement for access to signals from hundreds of rods, makes the AII amacrine cell and/or its gap junction with On cone bipolar cells likely sites of gain control.
source: The lack of transfer from rod to cone pathways, together with the requirement that the gain control mechanism have access to signals from hundreds of rods (Figure 8), makes the AII amacrine cell and/or its gap junction with On cone bipolar cells likely sites
evidence: This is inferred by combining multiple experimental constraints on the location of the gain control mechanism.

claim: Human behavioral threshold begins to increase for backgrounds near 0.01 R*/rod/s, similar to the backgrounds (~0.02 R*/rod/s) at which primate ganglion cell thresholds began to increase.
source: Human behavioral threshold begins to increase for backgrounds near 0.01 R*/rod/s, similar to the backgrounds (∼0.02 R*/rod/s) at which primate ganglion cell thresholds began to increase
evidence: This comparison is made between cited behavioral data and the experimental measurements from this study.

claim: The rate at which spontaneous activation of rhodopsin generates photon-like noise events in primate rods is 0.003–0.004 R*/rod/s.
source: the rate at which spontaneous activation of rhodopsin generates photon-like noise events in primate rods (0.003–0.004 R*/rod/s) (GD Field and F Rieke, unpublished)
evidence: This is stated based on unpublished data from Field and Rieke.

claim: The onset of behavioral and ganglion cell threshold increases is consistent with measures of the total noise generated by macaque rods.
source: They are, however, consistent with measures of the total noise (i.e., both discrete and continuous) generated by macaque rods (Schneeweis and Schnapf, 2000)
evidence: This is inferred by comparing threshold measurements to cited noise measurements.

claim: The gain of retinal signals measured via electroretinograms begins to decline only at backgrounds approximately fivefold higher than those that increase behavioral threshold.
source: the gain of retinal signals measured via electroretinograms begins to decline only at backgrounds ∼fivefold higher than those that increase behavioral threshold (Frishman et al., 1996)
evidence: This is cited from Frishman et al., 1996.

claim: Behavioral brightness matching experiments show a robust Rose–deVries region.
source: behavioral brightness matching experiments, which should be sensitive to changes in neural gain but not noise, show a robust Rose–deVries region (Brown and Rudd, 1998)
evidence: This is cited from Brown and Rudd, 1998.

claim: The spike responses of toad ganglion cells exhibit an approximately 10-fold range of backgrounds over which the threshold required to reach a criterion spike rate increases in proportion to the square root of the background.
source: the spike responses of toad ganglion cells exhibit an ∼10-fold range of backgrounds over which the threshold required to reach a criterion spike rate increases in proportion to the square root of the background (Donner et al., 1990)
evidence: This is cited from Donner et al., 1990.

claim: The region of the ganglion cell TVI curve with slope 0.5 was limited to a narrow range of backgrounds.
source: The region of the ganglion cell TVI curve with slope 0.5 was limited to a narrow range of backgrounds
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental measurements in Figure 3.

claim: Post-retinal mechanisms contribute substantially to the more extended Rose–deVries region measured in behavioral studies.
source: This suggests that post-retinal mechanisms contribute substantially to the more extended Rose–deVries region measured in behavioral studies
evidence: This is inferred from the difference between retinal measurements and behavioral measurements.

claim: Previously described gain control mechanisms are sensitive to variance.
source: Previously described gain control mechanisms are sensitive to variance (reviewed by Demb, 2008)
evidence: This is cited from a review by Demb, 2008.

claim: Some previously described gain control mechanisms act at locations with insufficient rod convergence.
source: act at locations with insufficient rod convergence (Dunn et al., 2006; Dunn and Rieke, 2008)
evidence: This is cited from Dunn et al., 2006 and Dunn and Rieke, 2008.

claim: Some previously described gain control mechanisms affect cone signals.
source: or affect cone signals (Dunn et al., 2007)
evidence: This is cited from Dunn et al., 2007.

claim: The novel gain control mechanism identified in this study is located in the AII amacrine cell or the synaptic connections it makes with cone bipolar cells.
source: The constraints above suggest a novel mechanism located in the AII amacrine cell or the synaptic connections it makes with cone bipolar cells (Figure 5)
evidence: This is inferred from multiple experimental constraints on the mechanism's properties and location.

claim: The site of adaptation in the rod bipolar pathway should be shared across ganglion cell types.
source: a location of the site of adaptation in the rod bipolar pathway indicates that it should be shared across ganglion cell types
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomy of the rod bipolar pathway which is common to multiple ganglion cell types.

claim: On midget ganglion cells adapted very similarly to On parasol ganglion cells.
source: On midget ganglion cells adapted very similarly to On parasol ganglion cells (data not shown)
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations, though the data is not shown.

claim: Retinal ganglion cells encode stimuli over 10 log units of background.
source: retinal ganglion cells encode stimuli over 10 log units of background
evidence: This is stated as a known property of retinal ganglion cells.

claim: The dynamic range of retinal ganglion cells far exceeds the dynamic range of any single gain control mechanism.
source: far exceeding the dynamic range of any single mechanism
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that multiple mechanisms are required to cover the full range.

claim: Backgrounds producing approximately 10–20 R*/rod/s halve the gain of the phototransduction cascade in primate rods.
source: Backgrounds producing approximately 10–20 R*/rod/s halve the gain of the phototransduction cascade in primate rods (Schneeweis and Schnapf, 2000)
evidence: This is cited from Schneeweis and Schnapf, 2000.

claim: Backgrounds producing approximately 0.4 R*/rod/s halve the gain of the rod bipolar to AII synapse by reducing the number of releasable vesicles.
source: Backgrounds producing ∼0.4 R*/rod/s halve the gain of the rod bipolar to AII synapse by reducing the number of releasable vesicles (Dunn et al., 2006; Dunn and Rieke, 2008; Oesch and Diamond, 2011)
evidence: This is cited from Dunn et al., 2006, Dunn and Rieke, 2008, and Oesch and Diamond, 2011.

claim: Backgrounds approximately 0.08 R*/rod/s engage a mechanism located downstream of the rod bipolar–AII synapse.
source: backgrounds ∼0.08 R*/rod/s engage a mechanism located downstream of the rod bipolar–AII synapse
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments in this study.

claim: The light levels at which the downstream gain control mechanism is engaged are consistent with backgrounds that are just detectable given the total noise generated by macaque rods.
source: the light levels at which this mechanism is engaged are consistent with backgrounds that are just detectable given the total noise generated by macaque rods (Schneeweis and Schnapf, 2000)
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the engagement threshold to cited noise measurements.

claim: At least five separate gain control mechanisms contribute to a single smooth function relating background to gain over more than 5 log units on each axis.
source: At least five separate gain control mechanisms that contribute to a single smooth function relating background to gain over >5 log units on each axis (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is inferred from the identification of multiple mechanisms and the smooth gain function shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The smooth functional form for adaptation relating background to gain was likely a target of selective pressure in primate evolution.
source: suggest that this particular functional form for adaptation was a target of selective pressure in primate evolution
evidence: This is speculated based on the coordinated action of multiple mechanisms producing a smooth function.

claim: Retinal gain controls operate at the lowest backgrounds physically possible.
source: retinal gain controls appear to operate at the lowest backgrounds physically possible
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that gain changes occur as soon as backgrounds are detectable above intrinsic noise.

claim: Each absorbed photon within the pool of rods providing input to an adaptational mechanism lowers gain.
source: each absorbed photon within the pool of rods providing input to an adaptational mechanism lowers gain
evidence: This is inferred from the rapid kinetics and low background levels at which gain changes occur.

claim: Adaptation at the rod bipolar to AII synapse approaches the sensitivity limit imposed by convergence and integration time.
source: Adaptation at the rod bipolar to AII synapse approaches the sensitivity limit imposed by convergence and integration time (Dunn and Rieke, 2008; see Figure 1B)
evidence: This is cited from Dunn and Rieke, 2008 and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: A single absorbed photon reduces the gain of the next single photon response at the rod bipolar to AII synapse.
source: a single absorbed photon reduces the gain of the next single photon response
evidence: This is cited as a property of adaptation at the rod bipolar to AII synapse.

claim: The onset of retinal gain control coincides with the dimmest detectable backgrounds given the intrinsic noise of the rods.
source: the onset of retinal gain control coincides with the dimmest detectable backgrounds given the intrinsic noise of the rods
evidence: This is concluded by comparing the background levels at which gain changes occur to the intrinsic noise levels of rods.

claim: All recordings were from On parasol ganglion cells in peripheral primate retina.
source: All recordings were from On parasol ganglion cells in peripheral (eccentricity typically >30°; ∼15° to 20° for the experiments of Figure 9) primate retina (Macaca nemestrina, fascicularis, and mulatta)
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Retina was obtained through the Tissue Distribution Program of the Regional Primate Center at the University of Washington.
source: Retina was obtained through the Tissue Distribution Program of the Regional Primate Center at the University of Washington
evidence: This describes the source of the experimental tissue.

claim: The retina was dark adapted for 1 hr while attached to the pigment epithelium.
source: The retina was dark adapted for 1 hr while attached to the pigment epithelium
evidence: This describes the experimental preparation procedure.
